title: Hamlet isometric town: production research
scope: A small, crafted architectural diorama for a future editable 3D town study. This is visual direction, not a claim about the current runtime or product implementation.

sources.title: Townscaper
sources.creator: Oskar Stalberg
observations: The direct-manipulation town reads because a limited set of roof, wall, bridge, stair and garden forms repeat with small contextual variation.
Water, streets and building footprints form the calm field; bright walls and roofs become the readable clusters.
The lesson for Hamlet is the rule system, not its saturated seaside palette or procedurally irregular coastline.

sources.title: Monument Valley
sources.creator: ustwo games
sources.kind: official game page and image gallery
observations: Large, quiet planes and high silhouette contrast make places legible before small decoration is read.
Colour is allocated by role: a muted environment, a small number of architectural accents, then a focused character cue.
Use its disciplined framing and colour hierarchy; avoid impossible-geometry puzzles, floating fragments and theatrical over-stylisation.

sources.title: Paperholm
sources.creator: Charles Young
observations: A thousand additions still read as one place because scale, material and proportion stay consistent while silhouettes vary.
The material reality is useful: thin overhangs, layered roof edges, chimneys, steps and openings create richness without busy texture maps.
For the town, put detail on roof lines, threshold pieces and small outdoor objects; keep broad wall faces almost plain.

sources.title: Three-Colour Houses
sources.creator: Charles Young
observations: The work uses constrained three-colour combinations and a roughly consistent physical scale to make variation feel authored rather than random.
Adopt a base material plus two controlled building accents per district, with a rare warm signal reserved for interaction or welcome.

sources.title: Cameras — Orthographic
sources.creator: Blender Foundation
observations: In an orthographic camera, objects retain apparent size at any depth and parallel lines do not converge.
Orthographic scale controls composition, so establish the visible town extent before changing model proportions.
Use a 45-degree world yaw and a 35.2644-degree downward elevation for equal-looking X/Y axes; adjust pitch only if people or façades become unreadable.

sources.title: Light Objects
sources.creator: Blender Foundation
observations: A Sun light provides uniform directional daylight; its rotation, not its position, sets direction.
Larger emitter size produces softer shadows and highlights. Use a broad key to retain a miniature daylight feel.
The documentation places typical Sun strengths around 250 W/m² for overcast daylight and 1000+ W/m² for direct sun; scene colour management and exposure still need visual tuning.

sources.title: Materials — settings
sources.creator: Blender Foundation
observations: Roughness controls the microfacet spread of specular reflection. Matte, high-roughness materials preserve shape and colour in a small mobile-friendly scene.
Keep walls, roads, plants and roof tiles non-metallic; reserve only a gentle lower-roughness accent for glass, wet paving or a vehicle windscreen.

sources.title: Ambient Occlusion Node
sources.creator: Blender Foundation
observations: Ambient occlusion represents local hemispherical blockage and is suitable for controlled contact separation.
It is not global dirt: apply a short AO distance so eaves, curbs, pots and feet anchor, while façades remain clear.

palette.principle: Warm neutral ground, desaturated blue-grey routes, quiet green planting, four identity accents, one only-for-meaning signal.

tokens.name: slate route
tokens.role: road or water strip, kept low-saturation

tokens.name: sage canopy
tokens.role: trees, greenhouse planting and garden beds

tokens.name: greenhouse glass
tokens.role: translucent glazing, never an opaque wall

tokens.name: ink
tokens.role: sign glyphs, seams and tiny contrast

allocation: About 60% warm neutrals, 20% green and slate environmental field, 15% building identity accents, and at most 5% high-attention warm signal.
Do not give each house an identity colour. The identity accent belongs to a destination, then repeats only in very small wayfinding details.

modeling_rules: Use a 1 m logical grid. A normal lane is 2 grid units wide; a small house footprint is 3 by 3 or 3 by 4; civic destinations span 5 to 7 units. Keep all footprints, curb radii and planting beds snapped to it.

Build the town in layers: base slab, route tiles, curb/edge, building shell, roof cap, threshold, then a limited prop kit. This lets a renderer swap or animate layers without baking the city into one mesh.

Every building needs one distant-read silhouette cue: a long mail slot and flag for post, a stepped book-stack roof for library, a north-light sawtooth or tall window band for studio, a striped awning for cafe, and a slender pitched glass volume for greenhouse.

Roofs are the main isometric detail carrier. Give each roof a visible fascia thickness, shallow overhang, ridge or parapet, two to five large tile/standing-seam breaks, and one functional interruption such as a chimney, skylight, gutter, planter or vent.
Keep façades to two visible material values: main plaster/wood and recessed opening. Model a shallow sill, door recess and canopy before adding decals or texture noise.

Props establish scale. Use simple people about 1.65 m high and cars/vans about 4.2 m long. A person should occupy roughly a doorway height; vehicles should take most of a one-lane road width, leaving an obvious walking edge.
Planting is clustered, not sprinkled. Use one tree family with three height variants, rounded crowns, a dark trunk/ground-contact shape, and garden beds that follow the street or building edge.
Use physical sign shapes first: small projecting blade, painted door plaque, menu stand, mail icon relief. Copy should be optional and legible only when the user is already close enough to act.
Avoid beveling every edge. Bevel only the silhouette or light-catching edges of roof slabs, curbs, awnings, signs and vehicle bodies; a uniform softening pass makes the town toy-like and loses craft.
Keep each destination useful at a glance. A town reader should identify the home, post, library, studio, cafe and greenhouse from roof/entrance/adjacent prop before reading a label.

camera: Default to orthographic, yaw 45 degrees and pitch 35.2644 degrees below horizontal. Lock the camera transform once the composition is accepted; move the town or use orthographic scale for reframing.
Frame a 12 to 16 building-town with a generous perimeter of ground plane so the diorama reads as an object, not as a cropped game map.
Maintain foreground-to-background height discipline: a tall civic building goes toward the top/back third, while key entrances face the lower-left or lower-right visible sides.
lighting: Use one soft, cool-white world fill plus one Sun key angled from upper left or upper right. Keep shadow direction consistent across all exports.
Give the Sun a modest non-zero angle for soft, clean shadows. Add one broad, weak area fill only if the unlit facade loses important entrances; it should not erase the key direction.
Use short-range AO/contact shadow only at feet, trees, curbs, porch posts, roof overlaps and vehicles. It should be perceptible when removed, not visibly painted on.

Prefer high-roughness (approximately 0.65 to 0.9) dielectric materials for plaster, timber, road and foliage. Glass can sit near 0.2 to 0.35 but must have visible thickness/tint and a dark inner frame to stay readable.
Test in a 1x image and a 0.5x image. If road seams, entrance depth and destination accents disappear at 0.5x, increase geometric separation before increasing saturation.

pitfalls: Do not treat an orthographic camera as a substitute for composition. A perfectly isometric view can still hide doors behind roofs or make streets feel like equal grey bands.
Do not use pure white walls, pure black outlines, fully saturated roofs, or strong bloom. Each destroys the material hierarchy and makes the town resemble a UI icon sheet.
Do not solve legibility with wordy signage. Repeated labels flatten hierarchy and create a theme-park feeling.
Do not use wide-radius AO or uniform dirty edge masks. The town should feel cared for, not weathered or game-grunged.
Do not give every roof the same pitch, chimney and dormer. Make a short set of roof families, then reserve a distinct interruption for civic buildings.
Do not let roads become an uninterrupted hard-surface grid. Break long routes with planted corners, benches, crossings, porch setbacks and tiny shared yards.
Do not let people, trees and vehicles compete with destinations. They are scale witnesses and movement cues, not collectible characters.
Do not bake signage, shadows or vegetation into a single building texture. Keep geometry/material channels separately editable for future interactive states.
first_scene_recipe: Make a 14 by 14 grid slab with a 2-unit loop road and one T junction.
Place the home near the lower-front route, the library at the back focal point, cafe and post on the junction, studio on a quieter side street and greenhouse at the planted edge.
Add one person, one seated pair, one bicycle, one small van, seven trees, three benches, two planters and a single lit welcome signal.
Render two test passes: clay materials with lighting only, then the restrained palette. Solve silhouette and contact before roof texture or signs.
